speaker: Karen
text: Good afternoon, and welcome to the lecture on renewable energy and storage.

speaker: Karen
text: Today we look at one community that is trying to run almost entirely on wind and sun.

speaker: Karen
text: The pilot project runs on an island in the North Sea, with about three thousand residents.

speaker: Karen
text: Being an island makes it a perfect test, because every unit of energy has to be accounted for.

speaker: Karen
text: Until recently the island relied on an old diesel generator and an undersea cable to the mainland.

speaker: Karen
text: The cable is ageing, and replacing it would cost more than the whole renewable project.

speaker: Karen
text: So the residents voted to see how far they could get on their own.

speaker: Daniel
text: Let us start with generation.

speaker: Daniel
text: The solar farm on the island produces about forty megawatts at its peak on a clear summer day.

speaker: Daniel
text: In winter that drops to a small fraction, so solar alone is never enough.

speaker: Daniel
text: The island also has six wind turbines along the western cliffs.

speaker: Daniel
text: The turbines are switched off when the wind speed rises above twenty five metres per second.

speaker: Daniel
text: That protects the blades during storms, which are common in autumn.

speaker: Daniel
text: On a typical day, wind and solar together cover most of the demand.

speaker: Daniel
text: The difficult days are calm, grey days in the middle of winter.

speaker: Daniel
text: Engineers call those periods dark doldrums, and every storage plan is built around them.

speaker: Karen
text: Generation is only half the story, the other half is storage.

speaker: Karen
text: The main battery uses lithium iron phosphate cells, which are safer and last longer than older chemistries.

speaker: Karen
text: It can supply the whole island for about four hours.

speaker: Karen
text: For longer gaps, the team experimented with green hydrogen.

speaker: Karen
text: Turning electricity into hydrogen and back again loses about a third of the energy along the way.

speaker: Daniel
text: Even so, worldwide, pumped hydro is still the largest form of energy storage by far.

speaker: Daniel
text: You pump water uphill when power is cheap and let it run down through turbines when it is needed.

speaker: Daniel
text: The island has no mountains, so that option was never on the table.

speaker: Karen
text: Now to demand, which is where the residents come in.

speaker: Karen
text: Most homes replaced their oil boilers with heat pumps over the last five years.

speaker: Karen
text: A heat pump moves about three units of heat for every unit of electricity it uses.

speaker: Karen
text: That makes electric heating far cheaper than it first appears.

speaker: Karen
text: Many residents also charge their cars at night, when the wind is often strongest.

speaker: Karen
text: A simple price signal tells their chargers when electricity is plentiful.

speaker: Karen
text: Shifting demand like this turned out to be cheaper than adding more batteries.

speaker: Daniel
text: One more technical detail, because it matters for the grid.

speaker: Daniel
text: The grid frequency in Europe is fifty hertz, and it must stay very close to that value.

speaker: Daniel
text: The battery helps here too, because it can respond in a fraction of a second.

speaker: Karen
text: Before we finish, your tasks for this week.

speaker: Karen
text: The homework is to estimate your own household's yearly electricity consumption from your bills.

speaker: Karen
text: Bring the number to the seminar, we will compare them.

speaker: Daniel
text: And a reminder about the essay competition.

speaker: Daniel
text: The prize this year is a visit to a geothermal plant in Iceland.

speaker: Karen
text: Thank you all, and see you next week.
